prompt: AKATA reports NPV 72534830.66 end-year and 70188970.32 mid-year on the real basis, and 69159247.46 mid-year on the nominal basis. What does the IRR read across those three runs?
options: 29.2361 percent end-year, and a lower root under mid-year, because the half-year shift discounts every receipt harder and the curve crosses zero sooner.
29.2361 percent on the nominal basis and 6.796117 percent on the real basis, since the real run discounts at the applied real rate.
29.2361 percent in every one of them.
Three roots, one per NPV.
explanation: The IRR is solved from the nominal flow vector alone, and neither the basis, the convention nor the discount rate enters that vector.

prompt: AKATA's NPV falls from 72534830.66 at 100 percent working interest to 18133707.67 at 25 percent, and the IRR stays at 29.2361 percent. Why?
options: Scaling every entry of a vector by one factor scales its NPV at every rate and leaves the zero where it was.
The IRR is solved on the gross revenue rows, which carry no capex, so no working interest can ever reach the root at all.
The engine solves the root on the discounted column, and the applied real rate of 6.796117 percent is the same in both of those runs.
The engine solves the IRR before the working interest is applied in the cascade.
explanation: The NPV is a reading of size and the IRR reports none of it: 18133707.67 and 72534830.66 sit under one root, and the take holds at 66.1723 percent throughout.

prompt: loss_making, [-1000, 500, 400], reports an IRR of -6.9926 percent. How should that be read?
options: As a failed Newton estimate that should have returned null, since the NPV is -100.00 at 0 percent and negative at every positive rate, so nothing brackets a root.
As a sign error in the report, because the vector never recovers its 1000 of outlay and a return on it cannot carry a minus sign.
As the rate at which the undiscounted total of the vector reaches zero, which is the payback reading rather than a root of the curve.
As a legitimate root: the rate at which a shrinking discount makes the receipts worth exactly the outlay.
explanation: The sampled curve reads 49.382716 at -10 percent and -100.000000 at 0 percent, so the crossing had to lie between them before any finder ran.

prompt: AKATA is on the real basis, so its discounted rows are the real flows 30821366.21 and 60767504.07. Which rate is its IRR of 29.2361 percent built to be compared against?
options: The applied real rate of 6.796117 percent, because that is the rate the real flows are discounted at and the IRR is a root of the same discounted column.
The nominal 10 percent, because the IRR zeroes the vector printed in money of the day, not the real flows.
Either rate, since the two bases give the same NPV of 72534830.66 end-year and therefore the same root.
The inflation rate of 3 percent, since the Fisher relation joins the two rates through it.
explanation: At the breakeven price of 64.916777 USD/bbl, where NPV is zero, the IRR reads 10.0002 percent: the nominal rate, which is the proof of which comparison it was built for.

prompt: late_payout, [-1000, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2500], reports a root of 20.1124 percent and prints the NPV there as -0.000000. What does that residual say?
options: Newton overshot on the flat part of the curve and the bisection fallback ran instead, which always leaves its residual on the negative side of zero.
The root actually sits between the sampled 4.693930 at 20 percent and -180.800000 at 25 percent, and the engine reports the midpoint of that bracket.
The engine prints the NPV at every reported root as a negative number, because the root is approached from above by convention.
The finder stops at a tolerance, not at an exact zero, and the rounded residual landed on the negative side.
explanation: Every reported root carries 0.000000 or -0.000000: conventional_five_year at 15.2382 percent and tiny_return at 0.1000 percent print the same kind of residual.

prompt: Before engines 3.10.0 the finder's method statement said Newton falls back to bisection when unconverged and returns null when no sign change brackets a root. What does bisection need before it can run?
options: Two rates with NPVs of opposite sign.
Every root of the curve, so that it can halve the interval between the two nearest and confirm that Newton reached the right one.
A vector with more than one sign change, on which it picks the root nearest zero on the positive side as the hurdle-rate answer.
A Newton estimate to refine.
explanation: two_roots_minus73_and_173 reads -6500000.000000 at -75 percent and 26500000.000000 at -50 percent, and that pair is a bracket; a curve that never changes sign gives it nothing.

prompt: no_real_root, [-1, 3, -3], changes sign twice, and its sampled curve reads -271.000000 at -90 percent, -1.000000 at 0, -0.250000 at 100 and -0.333333 at 200. Why is its IRR null?
options: Two sign changes always mean two roots, so this vector has two and the engine returns null with irrStatus multiple-roots.
Newton stepped from 10 percent into the region below -90 percent where the last entry dominates, and an unconverged Newton returns null.
The curve rises toward zero, touches nothing and falls back, so no sign change ever gives bisection a bracket.
The total at 0 percent is -1.00, and the finder is not run at all on a vector whose undiscounted total never returns its outlay.
explanation: Null here means no rate zeroes the vector, not that the vector is bad or good: it says nothing more than that the search found no crossing.

prompt: AKATA at 30 USD/bbl reports IRR null beside an NPV of -169873348.04. AKATA valued from 2030 with 2029 sunk reports IRR null beside an NPV of 206819768.67. What does the engine give a reader to tell those two nulls apart, and what does it still not give?
options: Nothing at all: both return a bare null, and only the NPV beside each one has ever distinguished them.
An irrStatus naming the branch that failed, which is not a verdict: the NPV beside each null is still the only thing saying one field is deeply uneconomic and the other worth 206819768.67.
A signed null, positive for the sunk run and negative for the price run, carrying the verdict without the NPV.

An irrStatus that names the branch and also grades the field, so a reader can rank the two runs from the status alone and never has to look at the NPV printed beside either one of them, whatever its sign.
explanation: Until engines 3.10.0 the null carried no status and the shapes were indistinguishable; the status names no-sign-change, no-root, multiple-roots or above-clamp, and none of the four says whether the field is worth anything.

prompt: AKATA reports IRR null with a 200000000 abandonment in 2035, and IRR null with a 60000000 abandonment as well. The two nulls have opposite causes. What are they?
options: With 200000000 the NPV is negative at every sampled rate, -58362170.82 at 0 percent, so nothing brackets a crossing; with 60000000 it is 81637829.18 at 0 percent and -78880508.48 at 100, so the curve crosses twice and the engine will not pick one of them.
They share one cause: a terminal negative flow always leaves the engine without a bracket, whatever the size of the abandonment.
Newton overshoots on the steeper curve of the larger abandonment, while the 60000000 root of 23.2570 percent sits above the top of the band.
The larger abandonment exceeds the 255000000.00 of capex it is set against, and the smaller leaves a last flow of -29598201.95 below the 2034 flow.
explanation: Until engines 3.10.0 the 60000000 run reported 23.2570 percent, one crossing of two; the engine now names a rate only where exactly one rate in the band from -99 to 1000 percent zeroes the NPV.

prompt: two_roots_2_and_6, [-100, 208, -108.12], has an NPV of -0.120000 at 0 percent, 0.036982 at 4 and -0.264463 at 10, and is zero at 2 percent and at 6. What does the engine return?
options: 6.0000 percent, the crossing Newton reaches climbing from its start at 10 percent, with no note that a second one exists.
2.0000 percent, the crossing nearest zero on the positive side, which is the hurdle-rate region a decision is made in.
Both rates, reported as a range running from 2.0000 to 6.0000 percent, since either one of them zeroes the NPV.
Null, with irrStatus multiple-roots and the crossings listed as 2.0000 and 6.0000 percent, because two rates in the band zero the NPV and it names a rate only where one does.
explanation: Until engines 3.10.0 it reported 6.0000 percent where the oracle read 2.0000 and the golden recorded a disagreement; the golden records none now.

prompt: A reader working from a pre-3.10.0 report takes three_roots_0_7_33's IRR of 7.3509 percent to a hurdle of 5 percent and approves. What went wrong?
options: The reader should have used the oracle's 0.0000 percent, which is below 5, and rejected the vector on the smaller root.
Nothing, since 7.3509 sits above the hurdle and the curve reads 0.081930 at 30 percent.
The NPV at 5 percent is -0.028075, negative; a hurdle comparison needs the sign of the curve at the hurdle, which is the NPV, not a root.
The engine should have reported 33, the largest root, and the reader should compare that with the hurdle instead.
explanation: On two_roots_2_and_6 the same reasoning happens to hold because the NPV at 5 percent is 0.027211, positive; the reasoning is wrong either way, and only the sign at the hurdle is an answer.

prompt: Why must a vector whose last entry is negative cross zero an even number of times, as two_roots_2_and_6 does?
options: Because the count of roots equals the count of sign changes in the vector, and a terminal negative after a positive middle makes two.

At very negative rates the factor on the last entry is enormous and drags the NPV down, -8832.000000 at -90 percent; at very high rates the NPV tends to the first entry, -100; negative at both ends and positive between means an even count of crossings.
Because Newton and bisection each find one root, and the engine runs both on a terminal-negative vector.
Because the terminal negative is discounted less than the outlay, making the curve symmetric about its peak at 4 percent.
explanation: no_real_root ends negative too and crosses zero times, which is also even: the argument fixes the parity of the count, not the count.

prompt: jv_analytic, [-12500000, 37500000], reports IRR 200.0000 percent and NPV 21590909.09 at 10 percent. AKATA reports 29.2361 percent and 72534830.66 at the same nominal 10 percent. A reader sorts the two by IRR. What has been measured?
options: How steeply each curve falls through zero, not how high it stands at the chosen rate; NPV ranks AKATA ahead.
The same thing either way, because both numbers are readings of one curve and the rankings must agree whenever the discount rate is the same on both sides.
Value per unit of capital, since 200.0000 percent reflects a 50000000.00 capex recovered in a single year against AKATA's 255000000.00.
The payback of each field, which is why jv_analytic at 1.333333 years ranks first.
explanation: IRR refuses to report scale: 200.0000 percent sits beside 21590909.09 and 29.2361 percent beside 72534830.66, and the steeper curve is the smaller field.

prompt: On the published multiyear_jv_real sweep the nominal discount rate runs from 0 to 20 percent and NPV falls from 148905488.72 to 50852201.45. What does the IRR read at the 20 percent point?
options: A root below 47.9020 percent, because the sweep at 20 percent applies a real rate of 16.504854 percent and the curve is read on harder-discounted flows.
Null, since at 20 percent nominal the NPV has fallen to a third of its 0 percent value and the sampled curve no longer brackets a positive root.
16.504854 percent, the real rate.
47.9020 percent, as at every other point.
explanation: The discount rate is the yardstick brought to the curve; the IRR is the property of the curve, and the sweep never touches the rows the curve is built from.

prompt: A manager asks whether AKATA survives a discount rate of 15 percent. Which single number answers, and what does the IRR of 29.2361 percent contribute?
options: The NPV profile point at 15 percent, 33900281.71, since the profile is the sensitivity to the rate and 15 is one of its sampled points on the real flows.
The IRR alone, because 29.2361 percent is the field's return and any rate below it is survived by definition.
The NPV at a nominal 15 percent, read from the discount rate sweep; the IRR only says how far the rate can rise before that NPV reaches zero.
The discounted payback at 15 percent, since a rate the field survives is one at which it still pays back inside its life.
explanation: The profile at 15 is on the real flows, where 15 is not a nominal 15; the sweep row is the reading at the rate the manager named, and the IRR answers how wrong the rate could be, not what the value is.
